## What you'll be able to do {#outcomes}

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Recognise the three ways you'll use AI in this course, and which to reach for.
- Ask an AI assistant for help on a synthesis task and **check its answer**.
- State and apply the rules that keep AI use responsible (verify everything; published
  data only).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Time:** ~30–45 min · **You'll produce:** a short note recording one thing the agent
helped with and how you verified it.
:::

## Why this matters {#why}

You'll work *with* an AI assistant from day one of this course — it can draft, explain,
and take busywork off your hands. But an assistant that is never checked quietly destroys
the very thing we care about: a trustworthy, reproducible review. So we learn to use it
*and* to verify it, from the start. This reflects the **RAISE** position that the
synthesist is always responsible, and every AI-suggested judgement is checked and recorded.

## The three surfaces {#surfaces}

You'll meet AI in three forms. Knowing which to reach for is the real skill:

1. **Chat advisor** — a chat window in your browser (e.g. Claude). It explains, drafts,
   and debugs, but can't see your files. Best for *learning and getting unstuck*.
2. **In-editor assistant** — GitHub Copilot inside VS Code. It sees the file you're
   working on and suggests as you type. Best for *working as you go*.
3. **Agent** — a tool (Claude Code) that runs in VS Code's terminal, can read and write
   your files and run steps for you. The most powerful, and the one we lean on most — used
   carefully.

We start with the chat advisor, because it needs no setup and is the safest way in.

## What you need {#prerequisites}

- VS Code installed (previous lesson).
- Access to an AI chat assistant in your browser (e.g. Claude at <https://claude.ai>).

## Walkthrough {#walkthrough}

1. **Open the chat advisor** in your browser and sign in.
2. **Ask it something useful for synthesis.** Try a real, low-stakes question, for example:

   > "I'm keeping screening decisions in a CSV file with columns study_id, title,
   > decision, reason, screened_by, date. Suggest three example rows for a review of cash
   > transfers and school enrolment."

3. **Read the answer critically.** Does it use the right columns? Are the decisions
   sensible? This habit — reading, not just accepting — is the whole point.
4. **(Optional) See the in-editor assistant.** If you installed GitHub Copilot, open a
   file in VS Code and start typing a comment like `# screening columns:` to watch it
   suggest. You can accept or ignore its suggestions.

::: {.callout-important}
**Two rules, always:**

- **Verify everything.** The agent drafts; *you* confirm it against a source or your own
  knowledge before you use or commit it. Never present AI output as trustworthy unchecked.
- **Published data only.** Only put public or already-published material into external AI
  tools — never confidential or unpublished data.
:::

## Try it yourself {#try}

Ask the assistant for help with one small, real task (drafting example screening rows,
explaining what a "commit" is, or rephrasing a sentence). Then write **2–3 sentences** in
a file called `agent-note.md`: what you asked, and *how you checked* the answer.

> **Done when:** you have an `agent-note.md` recording one use of the agent and your
> verification step.

## Verify {#verify}

Re-read your note. Could a colleague see *what* the AI did and *how you confirmed it*?
That short record is exactly the kind of documentation RAISE asks for — making AI use in a
review transparent rather than hidden.

## Common pitfalls {#pitfalls}

- **Trusting a confident answer.** Fluent does not mean correct — AI can invent facts and
  citations. Always check.
- **Pasting sensitive data.** When in doubt, leave it out; use only published material.
- **Over-relying.** Use the agent to go faster on things you can judge — not to make
  judgements you can't check.

## Recap {#recap}

You've met the three AI surfaces, used the chat advisor on a synthesis task, and practised
the core discipline: verify everything, published data only, and record what the AI did.
That discipline carries through every lesson from here.

## What's next {#next}

Now you'll put it together and make your **first version-controlled file** — your first
commit.
